I believe the qualities developed through athletics translate directly into this industry, and I am excited by the opportunity to learn from accomplished women leaders while building meaningful relationships with other driven student-athletes. Tell_us_a_little_about_yourself!:
My name is Amiya Stroumza, and in every sense of the word, I am an athlete.

Whether I’m sailing at a regatta or studying for an exam, I approach everything with discipline, grit, and determination. I am comfortable with the uncomfortable. I thrive in pushing my limits, embracing challenges, and proving to myself that my capabilities are limitless. I am used to failure, I am used to hating failure, and this is exactly where I create my successes. I know what it means to "fall forward," as Denzel Washington once said, and I have built my success on that very principle.

When I lost my fifth speech and debate tournament in a row in high school, I didn’t walk away—I reached out to every local TEDx conference and landed a spot as a speaker. Today, I help curate talks for TEDx@Stanford. When I lost my student body council election twice, I pivoted, ran for a position on the Parent Teacher Student Association (PTSA), and stayed on the board for four years, eventually becoming the first student president in San Francisco history, overseeing a $400,000 budget. When I faced rejection from every medical lab I applied to for my junior summer, I sent personalized emails to 80 labs in my city—one of them led to an incredible opportunity at UCSF in bioinformatics. To me, challenges are opportunities, and pressure is a privilege.

That mindset is what brought me to where I am today—a freshman at Stanford, studying Data Science and competing as a student-athlete on the Varsity Sailing Team. I wasn’t recruited. In fact, I made the decision to join a month into college, fully aware of the challenge ahead. But that’s who I am—I don’t shy away from challenges; I embrace them as chances to grow. I knew that in college, I didn’t want to live a life confined to a cycle of studying and academics. High school taught me that relentless work leads to results, but I also knew I wanted more. I wanted balance in my life.I wanted to strengthen my body, be outdoors in the sun, and work as part of a team.

Four months into being on the team, I can confidently say it has changed my life. Every day, it reminds me that hard work yields results. I never thought I’d wake up at 6 a.m. twice a week to work out, that I’d be able to do a pull-up, or that I could spend 10 hours a week on the water and still score above average on my math midterm—but I can. I did. And I will continue to push myself to do more.

The parallels between being a student-athlete and working in finance are striking. Both require relentless effort, the ability to create opportunities where none seem to exist, and the discipline to push forward when exhaustion sets in. Success in finance—just like in sailing—is about putting in the work, climbing the ladder, and stopping at nothing to achieve your goals. These principles guide me every day, shaping not just my work ethic but my outlook on life.

This is why I’m inspired to keep pushing, to keep discovering just how far my ambition, resilience, and determination can take me.

The Climb, Pause, Lift mantra is something I have lived by—climbing toward my goals, pausing to reflect on those who have supported me, and lifting others along the way.
